🚀 TradingAgents | ⚡ Installation & CLI | 🎬 Demo | 📦 Package Usage | 🤝 Contributing | 📄 Citation

🎉 TradingAgents officially released! We have received numerous inquiries about the work, and we would like to express our thanks for the enthusiasm in our community.

So we decided to fully open-source the framework. Looking forward to building impactful projects with you!

TradingAgents Framework

TradingAgents is a multi-agent trading framework that mirrors the dynamics of real-world trading firms. By deploying specialized LLM-powered agents: from fundamental analysts, sentiment experts, and technical analysts, to trader, risk management team, the platform collaboratively evaluates market conditions and informs trading decisions. Moreover, these agents engage in dynamic discussions to pinpoint the optimal strategy.

TradingAgents framework is designed for research purposes. Trading performance may vary based on many factors, including the chosen backbone language models, model temperature, trading periods, the quality of data, and other non-deterministic factors. It is not intended as financial, investment, or trading advice.

Our framework decomposes complex trading tasks into specialized roles.

Analyst Team

Fundamentals Analyst: Evaluates company financials and performance metrics, identifying intrinsic values and potential red flags.

Sentiment Analyst: Aggregates news headlines, StockTwits, and Reddit chatter into a single sentiment read to gauge short-term market mood.

News Analyst: Monitors global news and macroeconomic indicators, interpreting the impact of events on market conditions.

WeatherNext 2

This repo contains the code for WeatherNext 2 (WN2), the global, medium-range

atmospheric and cyclone forecasting model developed by Google DeepMind and

Google Research.

It also contains code for prior generation models

Accessing Forecast Data Feeds

If you are interested in directly accessing daily data feeds of WN2 model

outputs rather than running the model yourself, we provide them across multiple

Google Cloud

(including Earth Engine, BigQuery, and Vertex AI).

WeatherLab (including cyclone tracks).

OpenMeteo (including an API and interactive builder).

Model Guide & Documentation: Google Developers WeatherNext Guide

WeatherNext Cyclones Paper: Operational tropical cyclone forecasting

FGN/WN2 Technical Report: Skillful joint probabilistic weather

forecasting from marginals

(arXiv:2506.10772)

WeatherNext 2 Blog Post: WeatherNext 2: Our most advanced weather forecasting model

WeatherNext Cyclones Blog Post: WeatherNext: AI model achieves breakthrough in forecasting cyclones

Older Models

This repository serves as the primary home for the WeatherNext family models.

Alongside WN2, this repository also hosts the code and documentation for our

legacy and specialized models:

WeatherNext Graph : Deterministic

medium-range weather forecasting using graph neural networks. Published as

WeatherNext Gen : Diffusion-based ensemble

forecasting for medium-range weather. Published as GenCast.

Provided Pretrained Models

This repository provides code to run the different versions of WeatherNext 2 and

WeatherNext Cyclones. The only difference between them is that WN2 can also

predict 100m wind. In particular, WN2 also forecasts cyclones with the exact

same algorithm as WN Cyclones. Their weights are different due to independent

training runs.

WeatherNext 2

WeatherNext2_<2025 (Used Operationally): 0.25° resolution (~30km).

Fine-tuned on ECMWF HRES data and designed to be initialized directly from

operational HRES initial conditions rather than ERA5 reanalysis. Trained on

data through 2024. Corresponding weights files:

WeatherNext2_<2025_model{1,2,3,4}.npz .

WeatherNext Cyclones - models which reproduce the results in paper

WeatherNextCyclones_<2025 (Used Operationally): 0.25° resolution. The

model that ran live during the 2025 Atlantic hurricane season, publicly

referred to as FNV3 (NHC's postprocessed version was called GDMI). Trained

on data through 2024. The paper appendix contains a partial evaluation of

2025 in NHC basins for this model checkpoint, and how the tracker

improvement in September 2025 improved results. Corresponding weights files:

WeatherNextCyclones_<2025_model{1,2,3,4}.npz .

WeatherNextCyclones_<2024 : 0.25° resolution. Reproduces results from the

paper on 2024. Trained on data through 2023. Corresponding weights files:

WeatherNextCyclones_<2024_model{1,2,3,4}.npz .

WeatherNextCyclones_<2023 : 0.25° resolution. Reproduces results from the

paper on 2023. Trained on data through 2022. Corresponding weights files:

WeatherNextCyclones_<2023_model{1,2,3,4}.npz .

WeatherNext Cyclones Mini

WeatherNextCyclones_Mini_<2024 : 1° resolution. A lightweight version

suitable for lower memory and compute constraints (e.g., local testing or

single TPUs or GPUs). Not expected to match the performance of the larger

versions. Forecasts the same things as WeatherNext2_<2025, including

cyclones. Trained on data through 2023. Corresponding weights file:

WeatherNextCyclones_Mini_<2024.npz .

WeatherNextCyclones_Mini_<2023 : As above, but only trained on data through

2022. Corresponding weights file: WeatherNextCyclones_Mini_<2023.npz .

Evaluation results for WeatherNextCyclones_Mini can be found in the appendix

WeatherNext Cyclones Paper .

Quick Start Guide

The easiest way to get started with WeatherNext 2 is by running our interactive

Colab Notebook , which can be opened from

Colaboratory .

This notebook defaults to WeatherNext Cyclones Mini, which we recommend running

using the v5e-1 runtime, available for free as a Colab runtime. However, the

notebook can also be used to run the other models enumerated above (but these

will require a v5p accelerator).

In general, we recommend running WeatherNext 2 on TPU where possible, since its

implementation has been optimised for it. However, if choosing to run on GPU,

the attention implementation must be switched, as shown in the demo notebook.

The non-Mini models require H100 for sufficient VRAM. The Mini models should

manage inference on a P100.

Pre-trained weights and sample data are available on our Google Cloud

Inside the notebook, you will learn how to:

Automatically load the required model weights from our storage bucket.

Load initial state weather data (e.g., HRES initial conditions).

Initialize the WN2 (FGN) architecture.

Run auto-regressive rollout steps to generate a forecast prediction.

Visualize the outputs (e.g., temperature, wind speed, geopotential height).

Run the direct tracker on model outputs to obtain track data for cyclones.

Compute the training loss on model predictions and targets, and take a

gradient step.

Installation

This is research code provided as-is for the purpose of running and

experimenting with the published models. There are no guarantees of API

stability and future updates may introduce breaking changes without notice. We

recommend pinning to a specific release.

pip install git+https://github.com/google-deepmind/weathernext.git@v0.3.0

Model Weights

To run WeatherNext 2 or WeatherNext Cyclones, you will need to download the

pre-trained model weights. You can access the weights on Google Cloud

Code-Graph-RAG

Code-Graph-RAG parses a multi-language codebase with Tree-sitter, sharpened by compiler-grade frontends and runtime traces where available, builds a knowledge graph of its structure in an embedded graph database that needs no server, and lets you query, edit, and optimise that code in plain English. It works across a monorepo of mixed languages under one unified graph schema.

1. Index: cgr start --update-graph parses a repository into a knowledge graph (sped up)

2. Ask: cgr start answers questions and edits code, grounded in that graph

Latest News 🔥

MiniMax Models Added : Current MiniMax text models have been included.

See NEWS.md for the full history.

What It Does

Point Code-Graph-RAG at a repository and it reads every source file, extracts functions, classes, methods, modules, and the relationships between them, and stores the result as an interconnected graph. Once the graph exists you can:

Ask questions about the codebase in natural language and get answers grounded in the real structure.

Retrieve the actual source of any function, class, or method by name or by intent.

Edit code through the agent with AST-based surgical patching and a diff preview before anything changes.

Optimise code against language best practices or your own coding standards.

Find dead code by walking call and reference edges from entry points.

Search and rewrite structurally by AST pattern with ast-grep.

Overlay runtime behaviour: trace a test run (or pull production eBPF profiles) with cgr trace and merge the calls that actually happened into the graph, exposing dispatch that static analysis cannot see.

How It Works

The system has two components:

Multi-language parser. A Tree-sitter based parser reads the codebase and ingests functions, classes, methods, modules, and their relationships into the graph under a single language-agnostic schema. Where a toolchain is available, compiler-grade frontends layer exact facts on top (libclang for C/C++, go/types for Go, and opt-in Roslyn, javac and Jedi for C#, Java and Python), and dynamic tracing merges calls observed at runtime. Tree-sitter stays the backbone: a trace only sees code that ran, and a compiler frontend only covers what its toolchain can build.

RAG system ( codebase_rag/ ). An interactive CLI that turns natural language into Cypher queries, retrieves matching code, and drives AI-powered editing and optimisation.

<div class="snippet-clipboard-content notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="Source Code -> Tree-sitter Parser -> AST Analysis -> Knowledge Graph

User Query -> AI Model (Cypher Gen) -> Cypher Query -> Graph Results -> Response"> Source Code -> Tree-sitter Parser -> AST Analysis -> Knowledge Graph

User Query -> AI Model (Cypher Gen) -> Cypher Query -> Graph Results -> Response

The graph is stored in an embedded SQLite file by default. Memgraph and Neo4j are opt-in backends that run the same Cypher; Graph Backends compares them.

See the Architecture Overview and Graph Schema for the full picture.

Supported Languages

Python, TypeScript, TSX, JavaScript, Rust, Go, Java, C, C++, C#, PHP, Lua, Dart, and Julia are fully supported. Scala is in development, and Ruby, Kotlin, Swift, Elixir, Haskell, Solidity, Bash, and Nix have structural support (modules, functions, classes where the language has them, and imports) through the pluggable ast-grep tier. See the Language Support matrix for per-language capabilities.

T3 Code is an "agent harness control surface". It enables control of the agents on your machine with a best-in-class mobile app ( iOS , Android ), web app and Electron-based desktop app .

Works with your subscriptions on Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Grok Build, OpenCode, and Google Antigravity. If they're set up on your computer, T3 Code can control them.

"Wait, what are you selling me?"

Nothing. We built T3 Code because we wanted the best possible development experience with agents. We were inspired by existing solutions like the Codex desktop app, Conductor, Claude Desktop and Cursor Glass, but none met our bar.

We wanted something performant, remote-ready, and truly open. If we ever go the wrong direction, we want you to have everything you need to fork and build the editor that you want.

Installation

T3 Code currently supports Codex, Claude, Cursor, Grok Build, OpenCode, and Antigravity. Install and authenticate at least one provider before use:

Codex: install Codex CLI and run codex login

Claude: install Claude Code and run claude auth login

Cursor: install Cursor CLI and run agent login

Grok Build: install Grok Build CLI and run grok login

OpenCode: install OpenCode and run opencode auth login

Antigravity: enable it in Settings, then use Install Antigravity and Sign in with Google . No CLI is required.

curl -fsSL https://t3.codes/install.sh | sh

irm https: // t3.codes / install.ps1 | iex

Then run t3 to start the server and open the local web app. t3 service install keeps it running in the background, t3 update moves to a newer release, and t3 --help has the full reference.

To try it once without installing, run npx t3@latest instead.

Install the latest version of the desktop app from GitHub Releases , or from your favorite package registry:

Windows ( winget )

winget install T3Tools.T3Code

Windows ( scoop )

scoop install extras/t3code

macOS (Homebrew)

brew install --cask t3-code

Debian, Ubuntu ( .deb )

sudo apt install ./T3-Code- * .deb

Arch Linux (AUR)

yay -S t3code-bin

yay -S t3code-nightly-bin

The AUR packaging is maintained in this repository under packaging/aur .

Nix (nixpkgs)

nix profile add github:NixOS/nixpkgs/nixos-unstable#t3code

The package is maintained in nixpkgs

and includes the desktop app ( t3code-desktop ) and the t3 command.

See Nix installation for NixOS configuration and updates.

Broad native model support. This is a representative list; browse the workflow library for maintained, ready-to-run templates.

Image generation : Stable Diffusion 1.5, SDXL, SD3.5, Flux.1, Flux.2, Qwen Image, Z-Image, Hunyuan Image 2.1, HiDream, Lumina Image 2.0, Chroma, Anima, LongCat Image, Ideogram 4, Krea 2, MageFlow, Microsoft Lens, PixelDiT, Kandinsky 5, Ernie Image and Moss Image.

Audio generation : ACE-Step 1.5, Stable Audio 3, MiniMax Music 3 and Yue 2.

Built-in tools for inpainting, outpainting, reference conditioning, masks and compositing, model merging, upscaling, frame interpolation, segmentation, depth estimation, and media processing.

Save and load workflows as JSON, or recover complete workflows and seeds from supported generated media.

Runs fully offline: core does not download anything unless you request it. Use --offline to disable the optional paid Comfy API nodes and force all built-in functionality to stay offline, or --disable-partner-nodes to only disable the API nodes.

Support for saving and loading HDR videos and images in various formats.

Release Process

ComfyUI follows a weekly release cycle targeting Monday but this regularly changes because of model releases or large changes to the codebase. There are three interconnected repositories:

ComfyUI Core

Releases a new major stable version (e.g., v0.7.0) roughly every 2 weeks.

Starting from v0.4.0 patch versions will be used for fixes backported onto the current stable release.

Minor versions will be used for releases off the master branch.

Patch versions may still be used for releases on the master branch in cases where a backport would not make sense.

Commits outside of the stable release tags may be very unstable and break many custom nodes.

Serves as the foundation for the desktop release

Graph-Native Infrastructure for Context and Accountable AI Systems

Developer-first, knowledge infrastructure for AI, alternative to expensive enterprise platforms.

Ingest your enterprise data, extract what matters, build a Context Graph and knowledge graph (KG), and run graph analytics and causal reasoning over all of it, with full decision provenance baked in. Explainable, traceable, and trustworthy by design.

Context Management · Knowledge Modeling · Deterministic Reasoning · Ontology Management · Decision Intelligence · End-to-End Traceability

Open Source · Governed · Zero Vendor Lock-In

pip install semantica

English · Deutsch · Français · Español · Italiano · Português · العربية · اردو · हिन्दी · 中文 · 日本語 · 한국어

Knowledge Explorer · Context Graphs · Reasoning Engine · Decision Intelligence · Ontology Hub

▶ Watch the full platform walkthrough

Most AI agents run on embeddings, not meaning: similarity scores with no structure, no relationships, and no way to explain why a result came back.

Semantica is the semantic/context layer underneath your LLM, vector store, and agent framework: deterministic infrastructure (no LLM required for graph construction, reasoning, or provenance; where an LLM is used, it's optional and vendor-neutral, every major provider supported, OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, and more, via semantica.llms ) that turns fragmented enterprise data into a structured, queryable Context Graph and knowledge graph that carries the business context, not just the data structure. Ontologies and controlled vocabularies (OWL, SHACL, SKOS) make what an entity means to your business, its definitions, relationships, and rules, as explicit as the data itself, not just its embedding.

Decision provenance and audit trails aren't the product. They fall out of that structure for free, and in domains a regulator can question, the same structure that makes your agent smarter also gives you a straight answer to "why."

System-level explainability, not foundation-model explainability. Semantica doesn't expose or reconstruct what happens inside the LLM: its internal reasoning stays opaque, like it does for any external system. Semantica explains what's outside the model: the context fed in, the decision produced, its provenance, relevant relationships, applied policies, and the full execution trail.

Who it's for:

AI/ML platform teams shipping agents that make consequential decisions and need structured, queryable context, not just a vector index

Enterprise data teams on Databricks, Snowflake, or SAP turning tables already in the lakehouse or warehouse into a governed, lineage-tracked knowledge graph, without exporting to a third-party SaaS

Compliance, risk, and audit teams who need a straight answer to "why did the AI do that?" in a format a regulator accepts

Regulated enterprises (finance, healthcare, legal, government, defense) that can't ship a black box or hand their data to someone else's SaaS to get one

Platform and infra engineers who want the KG, reasoning, and provenance stack self-hosted and swappable, not locked to one vendor's backend

Data and knowledge engineers building a KG from messy, multi-source data, where conflicting facts get flagged and duplicates get merged, not silently overwritten

Context Graphs: A structured, queryable graph of everything your agent knows, decides, and reasons about

Decision Intelligence: Every decision is a first-class object: traceable, searchable by precedent, and causally linked

AI Governance & Ontology: SHACL constraints, conflict detection, compliance rules, OWL generation, and SKOS vocabularies, all with a visual editor

Full Auditability: W3C PROV-O provenance on every fact, exportable to JSON, CSV, or RDF

Deterministic Reasoning: Forward chaining, Rete network, Datalog, and SPARQL, with fully explainable paths, not black boxes

Knowledge Pipeline: Multi-source ingestion, entity-aware chunking, NER/relation/event extraction, and graph construction, with semantic dedup and provenance-preserving merges built in

Enterprise Data Platforms: Native connectors for Databricks (Unity Catalog + Delta Lake), Snowflake, and SAP OData, so data already in your lakehouse or warehouse becomes graph nodes with provenance, no export/import hop

Graph Analytics: Centrality, community detection, link prediction, and shortest-path queries over the graph you just built

Prime Agent: A Self-Improving RLM Harness

<a id="user-content-prime-agent-a-self-improving-rlm-harness" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink:

Prime Agent: A Self-Improving RLM Harness

" href="#prime-agent-a-self-improving-rlm-harness">

Documentation •

Prime Agent is an open-source coding and research agent for general and long-running work. It is designed around two core abstractions:

The Recursive Language Model (RLM) treats context as variables ( prompt-as-a-variable ) and tools like recursive subagents as function calls ( programmatic tool /sub-agent calling ) inside a persistent REPL.

The Continual Harness stores supplemental prompts, memories, skill descriptions, and reusable subagent specifications as durable state that Prime Agent can refine through small, evidence-backed updates, local to the session by default.

Install the latest stable version with the one-command installer:

curl -fsSL https://app.primeintellect.ai/prime-agent/install.sh | sh

On Windows, install from PowerShell:

irm https: // app.primeintellect.ai / prime - agent / install.ps1 | iex

The Windows installer downloads the latest stable Windows x64 build and verifies its checksum before installation.

Why Prime Agent

Prime Agent combines a persistent Python control environment with durable harness state, so useful working context and reusable operating patterns can outlive a single chat window.

Everything is programmatic: a persistent Python REPL is the built-in model tool; file operations, shell commands, tool use, subagents, and context management happen through code.

Subagents are built in: rlm.spawn(...) spawns real child agents for parallel or background work and returns their results programmatically.

The harness can improve: /refine reviews the current trajectory and can apply small, evidence-backed updates to supplemental harness state. It never rewrites the immutable base system prompt, and recorded snapshots support rollback.

Skills are executable: skills are importable Python packages, and the built-in skill creator can turn recurring workflows into project or personal skills.

Sessions run in the background: daemon-backed agents keep running when the terminal disconnects and can be reattached later.

Agents communicate directly: running agents can exchange messages and orchestrate one another without routing everything through the user.

Long tasks keep moving: automatic compaction, persistent goals, heartbeats, schedules, autonomous mode, and retained subagents preserve progress across turns and terminal sessions.

Connect Slack from /mcp or run /mcp login slack inside Prime Agent to search

your workspace and use Slack tools. See the Slack connector guide

for OAuth setup and troubleshooting.

Google Drive and Google Sheets

Connect Google's official Drive and Sheets MCP servers with your own Google

OAuth client: add them to mcpServers with clientId , clientSecret ,

callbackPort , and scopes , then run /mcp login <name> . See the

Google Drive and Google Sheets guide for the

Google Cloud setup and the tool mapping.

Clipboard over SSH and tmux

Prime Agent uses the local clipboard tool (such as pbcopy ) when available. In tmux it asks the attached tmux client to forward a clipboard buffer if that client advertises the Ms capability. This works with tmux's default set-clipboard external , unlike application-origin OSC 52. Without tmux, remote copies request delivery using OSC 52. Terminal requests cannot confirm that your local clipboard changed, so Prime Agent reports them as unconfirmed.

Nested tmux servers and terminals may still block delivery. An outer tmux with set-clipboard external can reject the inner server's OSC 52. In that case, run tmux set -s set-clipboard on on the outer server, or use native terminal selection (Shift-drag in most terminals; Option-drag in iTerm2) followed by Cmd-C. macOS Terminal.app does not support OSC 52; iTerm2 requires its “Applications in terminal may access clipboard” setting.

Custom certificate authorities

HTTPS requests trust your operating system's trust store together with the bundled Mozilla roots. For servers behind a custom CA, point NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS at a PEM bundle of your CA certificates — the same variable the Node/TypeScript build honors:

export NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=/path/to/your-ca.pem

Each transport reads the variable once when its first client is initialized. The background daemon keeps the environment it started with, so run prime-agent shutdown after changing it.

Getting Started

Start Prime Agent from the repository or directory you want it to work in:

<div class="highlight highlight-source-shell notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" dir="auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="cd /path/to/project

prime-agent"> cd /path/to/project

On first launch, run /login to choose a subscription or API-key provider. Prime Agent works in the current directory and can run commands and modify files there. Use a disposable clone, clean worktree, or another checkpoint you can inspect and restore.

LifeOS is a General Purpose AI Harness for doing anything you want to do in life and work with AI. It captures who you are, what you care about, and where you're trying to go, then uses AI that knows you to help you get there.

And because it has your full context, it makes everything you do more efficient and effective, from building apps, to starting a business, to creative projects… basically anything .

The whole system works on one central concept: moving from your Current State to your Ideal State — in pursuit of Euphoric Surprise.

⭐ If LifeOS is useful to you, star the repo

Stars help more people find the project and keep it moving. It takes one click.

Give it to your AI. LifeOS is installed by an AI, so the install is just a prompt. Paste this into your AI coding harness — Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Hermes, or any capable agent — and it does the whole setup for you:

Read https://ourlifeos.ai/install and install LifeOS for me.

Your AI reads the install page and walks the setup, asking permission before it touches anything.

Prefer the terminal? There's a one-line shortcut for Claude Code on macOS/Linux:

curl -fsSL https://ourlifeos.ai/install.sh | bash

Either path needs a capable AI coding harness — we build and run on Claude Code — and bun .

Core Components

The unique features — the parts you won't find anywhere else. Anything a good harness already provides on its own (built-in subagents, for example) isn't listed; this is only what LifeOS adds. See them live and click through on ourlifeos.ai .

LifeOS ships 97 public skills, from research, security, writing and art to video, publishing and your home. Browse them all on the site.

How is LifeOS different from using an AI harness on its own?

Your harness gives you raw capability. LifeOS is the layer on top that makes it yours — a system that knows your goals, people, and context, and keeps working toward them:

Persistent memory — Your DA remembers past sessions, decisions, and learnings

Custom skills — Specialized capabilities for the things you do most

Your context — Goals, contacts, preferences—all available without re-explaining

Intelligent routing — Say "research this" and the right workflow triggers automatically

Self-improvement — The system modifies itself based on what it learns

Your harness is the engine. LifeOS is everything else that makes it your car.

What harness does LifeOS run on?

Any high-end one. LifeOS is harness-agnostic by design — it's built on universal primitives (hooks, skills, context files, agentic routing), not one vendor's features. The code is TypeScript and Bash, and the core ideas — TELOS, the Algorithm, skills, memory — port to any capable agent.

Daniel builds and runs it on Claude Code , so that's the most-tested path today. But LifeOS isn't locked to it, and it's designed to run wherever your AI does.

How is this different from fabric?

Fabric is a collection of AI prompts (patterns) for specific tasks. It's focused on what to ask AI .

LifeOS is infrastructure for how your DA operates —memory, skills, routing, context, self-improvement. They're complementary. Many LifeOS users integrate Fabric patterns into their skills.

Recovery is straightforward:

Back up first — Before any upgrade: cp -r ~/.claude ~/.claude-backup-$(date +%Y%m%d)

USER/ is safe — Your customizations in USER/ are never touched by the installer or upgrades

Settings merge, not overwrite — The installer only updates identity and version fields; your hooks, statusline, and custom config are preserved

Git-backed — Version control everything, roll back when needed

History is preserved — Your DA's memory survives mistakes

[Bug] Compact Mach-O catalog omits slice-relative offset semantics #8302

[Bug] Compact Mach-O catalog omits slice-relative offset semantics #8302

opened on Oct 31, 2026

Issue body actions

Before submitting

I searched the open and closed issues for a related report.

I removed credentials, tokens, private paths, and sensitive target data.

MCP or agent integration

Observed behavior

With REA_MCP_OUTPUT_SCHEMA_PROFILE=compact , the real tools/list definition for inspect_macho does not say that normalized entrypoint, segment and section file offsets are relative to the selected Mach-O slice, while architecture offsets and Evidence locations are relative to the input container. The returned result identifies the selected slice and its container offset, but neither the compact output schema, tool description nor this result's limitations states how to combine those values. The full advertised output schema does contain the field descriptions, and the repository documentation explains the distinction.

Reproduction

On macOS arm64, using REA b43c329 and the TypeScript MCP SDK, I opened a self-built x86-64/arm64 universal AppKit executable, called tools/list , then inspect_macho({detail:"complete"}) in both full and compact output-schema profiles. The SDK explicitly validated both successful inspection responses using their advertised tool definitions.

For the selected arm64 slice the result reported container_file_offset: 32768 , __TEXT.vm_address: "0x100000000" , and __TEXT.file_offset: 0 . A known handler was at 0x100000784 : the corresponding slice-relative offset is 1924; adding the slice base yields container offset 34692. A local file read at 1924 returned 0000000000000000 ; offset 34692 returned ff8300d1fd7b01a9 , matching the same bytes in the selected thin slice. A separate successful Hopper-backed address_to_file_offset call returned container offset 34692, provider offset 1924 and image-base file offset 32768. The Evidence locations also used container offsets. The original app bytes were unchanged and not executed.

The full catalog schema included the descriptions Offset from the start of the selected Mach-O slice and Offset of the selected slice from the start of the input Mach-O container ; the compact advertised output schema included neither. The common tool description did not explain the bases. One full-profile Hopper mapping attempt independently failed before bridge readiness and reported cleanup incomplete; the successful compact mapping and separate source-byte comparison above are the controls used for this observation.

Expected behavior

Make the coordinate origins discoverable in the compact-profile workflow, for example with a short tool-description or result-level explanation, while retaining the existing exact schema and source values. The full schema and native investigation guide already document the intended distinction. Preserve unknown slice identity and mapping ambiguity rather than guessing an offset.

Impact and scope

A caller treating a slice-relative number as an input-file offset can inspect the wrong bytes. The example demonstrates the different bytes and absent catalog explanation; no autonomous agent decision or error rate was measured. This is a compact-catalog discoverability gap, not a claim that the normalized values are incorrect. One universal fixture and macOS host were tested; output-schema-off and other clients were not tested.

b43c329df779708e43ae297f498a844e45d9c923 source build; relevant inspection/schema/guide source was unchanged at origin/main 23de10bb2849cdce8ddbe70504aa7cc57de75a98 , which was not runtime tested.

Runtime and platform

Node 24.22.1, macOS arm64, TypeScript MCP SDK 2.3.1; Hopper was used only for the separate successful mapping control.

Target and artifact context

Self-built x86-64/arm64 universal AppKit executable, SHA-256 c90064a7d0ecf009323c54b36af3e6d1f7b8b8492a25ba4f8c26d3831ec57b70 .

Earliest failure stage

Transport or result projection

Relevant output or evidence

selected_architecture.container_file_offset=32768 ; normalized __TEXT.file_offset=0 ; address 0x100000784 ; slice-relative offset 1924; input-container offset 34692. Full versus compact inspect_macho output-schema JSON lengths were 28,147 versus 1,159 bytes for this catalog; these are bytes, not model-token or latency measurements.

Typed outcome or recovery expected

The offset basis should remain available to callers who select compact output schemas. Keep the explicit selected slice, existing container-based Evidence locations, and a clear way to distinguish source bytes from loader-adjusted memory.

Additional context

Related: #1973 fixed the previous missing selected-slice identity and full-schema descriptions; this report does not dispute that fix. #7155 concerns catalog size, and #8170 concerns source versus provider-memory byte reads. No unknown last-known-good version is asserted.

Acetone + methylmagnesium bromide, then acidic workup: what forms?

Acetone gives tert-butanol (2-methylpropan-2-ol), a tertiary alcohol . Methyl addition forms a new carbon-carbon bond. Acidic workup then protonates the resulting alkoxide to give the alcohol.

The reaction drawing shows acetone and methylmagnesium bromide forming tert-butanol after the two stages: ether, then acidic workup.

items.title: Rare Photographs Document the Scene Inside Hitler's Bunker in 1945
items.summary: Rare Photographs Document the Scene Inside Hitler's Bunker in 1945（来源：Hacker News）
items.content:
In the final days of April 1945, as Soviet troops fought their way into central Berlin, Adolf Hitler remained underground in the Führerbunker, a reinforced concrete shelter beneath the garden of the Reich Chancellery.

The German capital was collapsing around him, the Nazi leadership was in disarray, and the war in Europe was nearing its end. On April 30, Hitler and Eva Braun died by suicide inside the bunker.

Just days later, American photographer William Vandivert entered the captured complex and documented its rooms, abandoned belongings, and the wreckage of the Chancellery above.

His photographs, taken in the immediate aftermath of Berlin’s fall, preserve a remarkable record of the place where the Third Reich came to its end.

Oberwallstrasse, in central Berlin, saw some of the most vicious fighting between German and Soviet troops in the spring of 1945.

William Vandivert was a photojournalist who worked for LIFE magazine from the late 1930s through 1948. In the spring of 1945, he traveled to Germany to document the aftermath of the fighting.

Berlin had suffered months of Allied bombing before Soviet forces launched their final offensive against the city on April 16.

After two weeks of brutal street fighting, German resistance collapsed, and the Soviet Union took control of the capital on May 2.

Hitler’s bunker partially burned by retreating German troops and stripped of valuables by invading Russians.

Vandivert arrived shortly afterward and gained access to the remains of the Reich Chancellery and the underground bunker.

He became the first Western photographer to document the bunker’s interior after the fall of Berlin. A selection of his photographs appeared in LIFE in July 1945, while many others remained unpublished for decades.

The Führerbunker was part of a larger underground complex beneath the Reich Chancellery, the seat of Hitler’s government in Berlin. Its construction took place in stages.

A 16th century painting reportedly stolen from a Milan museum.

An earlier air-raid shelter, known as the Vorbunker, was built in 1935 and 1936 beneath a reception building at the Old Reich Chancellery.

As Allied bombing intensified, a deeper and more heavily protected structure was commissioned in 1943.

Construction began that year, and the main Führerbunker was officially completed in October 1944. The two shelters were connected by an underground passage, allowing occupants to move between them.

With only candles to light their way, war correspondents examine a couch stained with blood (see dark patch on the arm of the sofa) located inside Hitler’s bunker.

The main bunker was an extensive reinforced-concrete structure, with its floor approximately nine meters below ground.

Its exterior measured roughly 27 meters long and 22 meters wide, while its ceiling and outer walls were approximately 3.5 meters thick.

The complex contained offices, private living quarters, bedrooms, bathrooms, a kitchen, a medical room, and conference facilities.

Abandoned furniture and debris inside Adolf Hitler’s bunker, Berlin, 1945.

Hitler’s private quarters included a bedroom and sitting room, while Eva Braun had separate accommodation nearby.

There were also rooms for military personnel, security staff, and other members of the Nazi leadership.

Although heavily fortified against aerial attacks, the bunker was a confined underground environment with no natural daylight, relying on artificial lighting and ventilation.

Papers (mostly news reports dated April 29, the day before Hitler and Eva Bruan killed themselves) inside Hitler’s bunker, Berlin, 1945.

Hitler moved into the Führerbunker on January 16, 1945, as the military situation deteriorated rapidly.

From there, he continued receiving reports from the front and issuing orders to German commanders, even as Soviet forces advanced toward the capital.

By April, the Red Army had reached the outskirts of Berlin and launched its final offensive on April 16.

Soviet troops encircled the city on April 25 and pushed toward the government district, where German soldiers, members of the Volkssturm, and Hitler Youth units attempted to resist the advancing forces.

A Russian soldier stands in Adolf Hitler’s bunker, Berlin, 1945.

Fighting continued through the streets, often from building to building, while civilians struggled to find shelter amid the bombardment.

On April 29, Hitler married Eva Braun in a small ceremony inside the bunker. The following afternoon, April 30, both died by suicide in Hitler’s private quarters.

Hitler shot himself, while Braun took cyanide. Their bodies were carried into the garden of the Reich Chancellery and burned by members of Hitler’s staff.

Desk inside Adolf Hitler’s bunker, Berlin, 1945.

Soviet troops were already fighting close to the complex, and the collapse of the Nazi leadership was only days away.

Berlin’s remaining German forces surrendered on May 2, bringing the battle for the capital to an end. Germany’s unconditional surrender followed on May 7 and 8, 1945, marking the end of the war in Europe.

An SS officer’s cap, with the infamous death’s-head skull emblem barely visible.

When Vandivert entered the complex, the rooms offered a revealing picture of the final hours of the Nazi leadership.

Furniture, personal belongings, scattered papers, and other objects remained among the damaged interiors. Soviet soldiers had already searched parts of the structure, and the rooms showed signs of destruction and disorder.

Vandivert documented the private quarters, the conference areas, and the surroundings of the Chancellery.

A ruined, empty and likely looted safe inside Hitler’s bunker.

In his notes to LIFE editors in New York, he also described the conditions under which he photographed the interior, including the use of a candle to illuminate some of the dark rooms.

The destruction above ground was equally extensive. The New Reich Chancellery, Hitler’s imposing government headquarters, had been heavily damaged during the fighting and was later demolished.

MCP or agent integration

Observed behavior

trace_native_values conflates node-page omission with traversal truncation in truncated . Its last page has truncated: true whether the whole graph was explored or a node/edge budget stopped traversal. In the tested node- and edge-cap cases next_offset was null , unknowns was empty, and the only budget limitation was a generic list of possible limits. The caller cannot tell from the final page whether the assembled pages exhaust the explored graph or a traversal budget stopped collection early.

Reproduction

Using real Ghidra 12.1.4 over stdio MCP on a source-owned arm64 Mach-O, open the target and trace _evaluate with max_depth: 1 , max_functions: 4 , max_call_sites: 20 :

With max_nodes: 100 , max_edges: 200 , limit: 100 , the result has 19 nodes, 17 edges, truncated: false , next_offset: null , and no unknowns.

With the same budgets, limit: 3 and offset: 18 , the last page has one node, total_nodes: 19 , truncated: true , next_offset: null , and no unknowns. Walking all seven pages recovered all 19 node IDs and 17 edges for this fixture.

With max_nodes: 5 , max_edges: 200 , limit: 3 , offset: 3 , the last page has two nodes, total_nodes: 5 , truncated: true , next_offset: null , and no unknowns. With max_edges: 1 , max_nodes: 100 , limit: 3 , offset: 12 , the last page similarly reports truncated: true , no next page and no unknowns; the trace has 14 nodes and one edge.

Controls with max_depth: 0 and max_functions: 1 reported explicit call-depth and decompilation-budget unknowns respectively. Unpaged node- and edge-capped requests also returned truncated: true without a specific unknown.

These are one fixture and host. The default output is not claimed to be truncated on arbitrary targets. Pagination re-runs analysis; no cross-mutation snapshot consistency is claimed here.

Expected behavior

Expose separately whether the returned page omits retained graph rows and whether the underlying traversal was incomplete, with specific observed truncation reasons where available. An agent should be able to decide whether to follow next_offset , increase a particular budget, or treat the examined graph as exhausted. Keep explicit unknowns, bounded allocation, existing usable rows and per-page provenance. This is a proposed contract improvement; the current single boolean is what was observed.

Impact and scope

Without a distinct traversal-completeness result, a consumer assembling pages cannot reliably decide whether the assembled graph is complete under the requested depth and other limits. Node and edge total_* fields count retained rows, not an independently known total beyond a cap. CLI behavior, other providers, output-byte limits and interruption are untested.

“Performance” Oryon: Qualcomm’s Little Core

Oct 24, 2026

Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X2 Elite uses a hybrid core setup, breaking away from the all-big-core strategy that the company previously used with in-house core designs. The Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme X2E96100 contains 18 cores, divided into 6 “performance” cores and 12 “prime” cores. Qualcomm’s “performance” cores fill the same role as little cores or efficiency cores on other chips, so I’ll be calling them E-Cores for simplicity. Like E-Cores on other chips, Qualcomm’s E-Cores are optimized for lower power and performance points than their big-core counterparts. These smaller cores can contain background tasks and lightweight applications that don’t require maximum performance, which saves power by not waking up the big cores. Under heavy multithreaded workloads, the E-Cores can step in to boost overall throughput.

Here, I’ll be looking at Qualcomm’s E-Core architecture in the Asus Zenbook A16 UX3607OA, which Asus has kindly sampled.

Core Overview

Qualcomm’s E-Core is a 4-wide out-of-order architecture running at 3.6 GHz, making it a modest affair next to the likes of Intel’s Skymont, or even the older Crestmont architecture used in Intel’s last-gen Meteor Lake chip. But despite being “only” a 4-wide core, Qualcomm’s E-Core can still punch pretty hard thanks to a combination of good branch prediction, substantial backend resources and large, low-latency caches.

On the instruction set side, Qualcomm’s E-Cores support SVE2 and SME to maintain consistent ISA extension support across the chip. Both features are new to the Snapdragon X2 Elite, since Qualcomm’s prior Snapdragon X Elite lacked SVE support. Besides vector extensions, Qualcomm supports a grab bag of security-focused ISA extensions like pointer authentication and memory tagging (MTE).

Frontend: Branch Prediction

Branch prediction can heavily affect both performance and power efficiency, so even density optimized cores have to make substantial investments into fast and accurate branch prediction. For their E-Core, Qualcomm has decided on a branch predictor that does well on the basics, but doesn’t incorporate some of the bling seen on the latest branch predictors on recent AMD, Arm, and Intel cores. A 1024 entry branch target buffer (BTB) is fast enough to deliver back-to-back predictions for taken branches. Intel and AMD’s big cores as well as density optimized cores from Arm like the Neoverse N2 can do two taken branches per cycle. Unlike Qualcomm’s prior Oryon core in the Snapdragon X Elite, the 1024 entry BTB here seems to be decoupled from the L1 instruction cache. Measured capacity doesn’t vary depending on code footprint or branch spacing.

Throughput drops to one taken branch every three cycles once the test spills out of the 1024 entry BTB, with another slowdown visible after exceeding the 128 KB L1 instruction cache’s capacity. Qualcomm might be using a second level BTB tied to the instruction cache, or could even be calculating direct branch destinations as those instructions arrive at the decoder. While doing so is simpler and more area efficient than implementing a very large L2 BTB, it does mean the branch predictor can’t follow taken branches after an instruction cache miss. That could limit the core’s ability to accurately prefetch instructions over large code footprints.

For direction prediction, Qualcomm’s E-Core can recognize fairly long patterns and handle a lot of them. The core can track roughly 16K patterns with 512 branches in play, or somewhere around 1K patterns with a single branch. Prediction accuracy across Geekbench 7’s workloads is roughly on par with Arm’s Neoverse N2, and better than Arm’s Neoverse N1.

A 40 entry return stack helps predict returns, and can sustain a call+return pair every two cycles. That’s a taken branch every cycle on average, making Qualcomm’s return stack faster than the one on AMD’s Zen 5 or Intel’s Skymont. In capacity terms, Qualcomm’s return stack lands in the middle of the pack. It’s much smaller than the 128 entry structure in Intel’s Skymont and Crestmont, but larger than the 24 entry one on Lion Cove.

Capacity has to be taken in context though. Some cores like Intel’s Lion Cove seem to fall back to an alternate predictor on a return stack underflow, letting them avoid mispredicts. Qualcomm’s E-Core and Intel’s Skymont in contrast see taken branch latency rise to over a dozen cycles, which is high enough to indicate mispredicts. It’s a story of different designs striking a balance in different ways. One approach is to design a small return stack with only a minor penalty on underflow. Another is to create a larger return stack so you only have to worry about the underflow case once in a blue moon. Qualcomm is leaning towards the latter. A 40 entry return stack should be plenty, though it stops short of Skymont’s crazy structure.

Frontend: Instruction Fetch

Qualcomm strikes a similar balance with the instruction cache. A 128 KB instruction cache is much larger than the 64 KB or 32 KB ones found on contemporary designs, which helps the core avoid having to fetch instructions from L2. If code does spill out to L2, frontend bandwidth drops to about two instructions per cycle. It’s not bad, but it is lower than what Skymont can sustain from its shared L2.

The L2 cache acts like a last level cache for the CPU, so missing it leads to very poor instruction bandwidth.

The AI coding agent that answers the question.

Chat in the browser

Praex is an open source (MIT) AI coding agent for the terminal. It reads your codebase, edits files, runs commands, and keeps sessions you can come back to. Use it with your own key for any major provider or with a model running on your own machine. No Praex account is needed for either.

curl -fsSL https://praex.ai/install.sh | bash

Prebuilt binaries for Linux x64 and macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel), with SHA256 checksums, are also on the Releases page.

Use your own key

Set the provider's usual environment variable and start Praex:

<div class="highlight highlight-source-shell notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" dir="auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... # or OPENAI_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY, ...

praex"> export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... # or OPENAI_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY, ...

Or store a key with praex auth login . Works with OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Groq, DeepSeek, Mistral, OpenRouter, xAI, and any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. praex models lists what is available. Usage with your own key is unlimited and free.

Local models

Point Praex at Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, vLLM or any other OpenAI-compatible server. Put this in praex.json in your project (or in ~/.config/praex/praex.json for every project):

<div class="highlight highlight-source-json notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" dir="auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="{

"$schema": "https://praex.ai/config.json",

"provider": {

"npm": "@ai-sdk/openai-compatible",

"name": "Ollama (local)",

"options": { "baseURL": "http://localhost:11434/v1" },

"models": { "qwen3-coder:30b": { "name": "Qwen3 Coder 30B" } }

"$schema" : " https://praex.ai/config.json " ,

"provider" : {

"ollama" : {

"npm" : " @ai-sdk/openai-compatible " ,

"name" : " Ollama (local) " ,

"options" : { "baseURL" : " http://localhost:11434/v1 " },

"models" : { "qwen3-coder:30b" : { "name" : " Qwen3 Coder 30B " } }

Praex hosted models (optional)

Praex also runs hosted models we post-train and serve on our own GPUs. Sign in with praex login to use them:

fast daily driver

heavier coding and reasoning

frontier-class flagship

No nannying. Praex models answer the question without moralizing, lecturing, or refusing legitimate work. There is a hard floor for genuinely dangerous content, and nothing else.

TUI built for real work: folded tool output, sessions, themes

Permission modes · manual approval by default, loosen when you trust it

Headless runs · praex run "fix the failing test" for scripts and CI, praex serve for a local server

/rc · Remote Control: keep a session running here and continue it from your phone or the web (Praex account)

Web search on hosted tiers, permission-gated per query

Memory · persistent per-user memory across sessions

Build from source

Requires Bun .

<div class="highlight highlight-source-shell notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" dir="auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="bun install

cd packages/opencode

bun run script/build.ts --single

./dist/opencode-linux-x64/bin/opencode --version"> bun install

cd packages/opencode

bun run script/build.ts --single

./dist/opencode-linux-x64/bin/opencode --version

Built on OpenCode

Praex is a fork of OpenCode (MIT). We keep its excellent agent core, including support for every provider above, and add our own work on top: stricter permission checks for destructive commands, an agent loop that carries on when a step stalls, a self-check after headless runs, Remote Control (/rc), persistent memory, and optional hosted Praex models. Upstream attribution is preserved in LICENSE and THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md .

Election 2026 Policy

Here’s why you can’t shake those unhinged political texts

You might be receiving political texts even if you’ve never made a political donation.

You might be receiving political texts even if you’ve never made a political donation.

by Lauren Feiner

Oct 31, 2026, 12:00 PM UTC

Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images

Lauren Feiner is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform.

“Its James Talarico. Can you please please please please pretty pretty please rush in even just $1?”

“Who’s working to elect James Talarico? Marxists.”

“Wow! Wow! Wow! Mark Kelly just made a HUGE announcement!”

“We asked Ben Verlander, MLB analyst and former Tigers prospect, to record a quick video about the election this Tuesday, November 3rd.”

“See which of your friends or family members have voted in the past and remind them to vote this year.”

If any of these messages sound familiar, it’s likely because they’re part of the massive stream of text messages flooding your phone leading up to the US midterm elections on Tuesday. The scale of the issue is not entirely clear, but call-blocking company Robokiller found that 15 billion political texts were sent in 2022, thanks in part to a Supreme Court decision the year prior that made it easier to send some mass calls and texts without consent. Alex Quilici, CEO of spam protection service YouMail, has an even higher estimate of 25 billion to 30 billion political texts this year, but caveats it’s an informal approximation. The volume is about the same to 10 percent higher than in 2024, he says.

There’s some good news and some bad news about these messages, says PIRG consumer watchdog director Teresa Murray. “The bad news is that political calls and political texts are exempt from the do-not-call-list rules,” Murray says. “The good news is that the election is next Tuesday, and hopefully within a few days after that, we’ll know what the results are and there won’t be any need to have any texts, or calls, or emails anymore after that.”

There are still some things consumers can try to stem the flow of these messages blowing up their phones — but it likely won’t significantly reduce it before Tuesday.

“In between all of the ‘legitimate’ political texts … there are going to be some scams in there”

The simplest thing you can do is send “stop” or block and report the messages as spam, which will notify your service provider of a likely spam number. That probably won’t result in any immediate change, Murray says, but if enough people report the same number in a certain period of time, the provider might begin to block it or label it as spam. You can also file a complaint with the Federal Communications Commission or your state attorney general if you believe a number is using an autodialer without your consent — something that even the people behind political texts are not supposed to do. Whatever you do, Murray says, do not click any links you receive from numbers you don’t know.

“In between all of the ‘legitimate’ political texts that are going out to support this candidate, or vote against that candidate, or vote for this issue, or whatever, there are going to be some scams in there,” Murray says. “If you want to donate money at this point, I would recommend going directly to the website for that political candidate, or for that PAC, and donating it that way.”

How did all of these campaigns get your number in the first place? If you’ve donated to a political candidate or issue group, that might seem obvious. But campaigns are also likely getting your information — including details about whether you might be likely to contribute to or vote for their candidate or issue — through data brokers that have nothing to do with politics. Data brokers collect and sell information from both public and private sources, such as public voter rolls, your online behavior observed by advertising web trackers, and loyalty programs. By collating all of this information, campaigns can try to infer your behavior, though they also might end up with outdated info, like old addresses that lead you to getting texts about a state you no longer live in (or even erroneous info that invites them for states you never lived in).

“As a consumer protection advocate, it’s so frustrating to have to say, ‘What can each individual person do?’”

“Errors in the processing of this information and the identification of individuals are very prevalent,” says Sara Geoghegan, consumer privacy program director of the Electronic Privacy Information Center. “Sometimes multiple people use the same device. Sometimes people have similar names. Sometimes people move. And this is such an unregulated ecosystem that there aren’t really rules in place to make sure that this is being effective and accurate, let alone free from bias, discrimination, and verified for privacy impact before processing this information.

“As a consumer protection advocate, it’s so frustrating to have to say, ‘What can each individual person do, and how many numbers do they need to block, and what are the toggle and privacy settings that they should toggle on?’” Geoghegan says. Meanwhile, “the companies that are trading in our most sensitive information are the ones who should stop harmful surveillance and the use of harmful technologies to have us better engage civically with our society, and not the other way around,” she says.

“I’ve spoken to people, someone last week who said, ‘Why would I even donate again when I get put on all these lists?’”
